children.label: Week 1: Introduction
children.definition: Introduction to medical imaging: anatomical vs functional imaging, why we image, the DICOM standard, body planes, and how to measure the efficiency of a predictive model.

children.label: Anatomical imaging
children.definition: Provides information about the **anatomy or structure** of the body.

children.label: X-rays
children.definition: X-ray beams are absorbed differently by various structures in the body, such as bones and soft tissues. This property is used to recreate an image of the inner body.

children.label: Computed Tomography (CT)
children.definition: Uses x-ray techniques to create 2D and 3D images of the body. More detailed than plain x-rays, and better for analysing soft tissues.

children.label: MRI (T1 / T2)
children.definition: T1- and T2-weighted MRIs are considered anatomical imaging. Uses strong magnetic fields ($\vec{B}_0$) and radio waves to create pictures of internal body structures.

children.label: Ultrasound
children.definition: Uses high-frequency sound waves and a handheld transducer to create real-time, non-invasive images of soft tissues.

children.label: Optical imaging (OCT)
children.definition: A diverse class of light-based techniques used to capture structural, functional and anatomical information of biological tissues. Includes OCT (optical coherence tomography).

children.label: Functional imaging
children.definition: Detecting or measuring changes in **metabolism, blood flow, regional chemical composition and absorption**.

children.label: Positron Emission Tomography (PET)
children.definition: Uses radioactive substances known as radio-tracers to visualise and measure changes in metabolism.

children.label: SPECT
children.definition: Single photon emission computed tomography. A 3D reconstruction is made from injected radio-tracers and gamma detection.

children.label: Optical fluorescence
children.definition: Tracks biological activity by measuring light emitted from fluorescent indicators.

children.label: Functional MRI (fMRI)
children.definition: Measures and maps brain activity by detecting changes in blood flow.

children.label: Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI)
children.definition: Advanced MRI that uses the micro-structural movement of water molecules to visualise white matter tracts and neural pathways in the brain.

children.label: Purpose of medical imaging
children.definition:
Medical imaging has four main purposes:

- Diagnosis
- Research
- Preoperative surgical planning
- Image guided therapy

children.label: Diagnosis
children.definition: Using images to diagnose disease.

children.label: Research
children.definition: Provide information to study anatomical and functional structures for research purposes.

children.label: Preoperative surgical planning
children.definition: Using images to plan a surgery before it happens.

children.label: Image-guided therapy
children.definition: Using images to guide a treatment as it is delivered, like cancer treatment.

children.label: DICOM format
children.definition: **Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine**: the standard to treat medical images. The communication is based on TCP/IP.

children.label: Body planes
children.definition: Imaginary planes that cut the body into sections so images can be described consistently. There are three standard planes.

children.label: Sagittal plane
children.definition: Divides the body into left and right parts.

children.label: Coronal plane
children.definition: Divides the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior) parts.

children.label: Axial (transverse) plane
children.definition: Divides the body into upper (superior) and lower (inferior) parts.

children.label: Efficiency of predictive modelling
children.definition: Measuring how good a predictive model or test is, using the counts in the confusion matrix.

children.label: Confusion matrix
children.definition:
| | Truth: Positive | Truth: Negative |
|---|---|---|
| **Test: Positive** | TP | FP |
| **Test: Negative** | FN | TN |

TP = true positive, FP = false positive, FN = false negative, TN = true negative.

children.label: Sensitivity
children.definition:
True positive rate: of all truly positive cases, the fraction the test catches.

$$\text{Sensitivity} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$

children.label: Specificity
children.definition:
True negative rate: of all truly negative cases, the fraction the test correctly clears.

$$\text{Specificity} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}$$

children.label: PPV
children.definition:
Positive predictive value (precision): given a positive test, the probability the case is truly positive.

$$\text{PPV} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$$

children.label: NPV
children.definition:
Negative predictive value: given a negative test, the probability the case is truly negative.

$$\text{NPV} = \frac{TN}{TN + FN}$$

children.label: Week 2: MRI
children.definition: Magnetic Resonance Imaging

children.label: Hydrogen Atoms
children.definition:
MRI uses $^1\mathrm{H}$ nuclei to change its magnetic field direction

$\mathrm{H}$ is used over other atoms because:

- Biological tissues contain many $^1\mathrm{H}$
- is the only major atom that is MR sensitive
- Most abundant atom in the body
- majority of hydrogen is in water
- Essentially all MRI is hydrogen imaging

children.label: Precession
children.definition:
Imagine a spinning top leaning at an angle: its axis sweeps around the vertical, tracing a cone. That motion is **precession**

![Precession](/images/c2a686dd6a03c48e.png)

children.label: Larmor Frequency
children.definition:
Precession occurs at the **Larmor frequency**. Therefore we can define it as **the rate or frequency of this precession wobbling motion**:

$$
\omega_0=\gamma B_0
$$

children.label: Radio Frequency pulses at Larmor frequency
children.definition: When applying a RF pulse perpendicular to $B_0$ at $\omega_0$, the magnetic moments of the nucleis Tilt to the transverse plane (away from $B_0$). Therefore net magnetic moment turns towrds the $xy$ plane.

children.label: Precession in/out of phase
children.definition:
- When protons precess together, we say that they are in phase
-When protons precess separately, we say that they are out of phase

![precession on phas and out of phase](/images/32b6e8dd0606a318.png)

children.label: Magnetic Moment
children.definition:
Informal definition: "Tells us how strong a tiny magnet is and which way it points"

We represent it with an arrow "$\mu$". For a proton, its directly proportional to spin:

$$
\mu=\gamma S
$$

Where $\gamma$ is **gyromagnetic ratio**, a specific constant of a particle. For a proton its positive.

![magneticMoment](/images/21cf55c3f899ee04.jpg)

children.label: Spin
children.definition:
In mechanics, a rotating object has angular momentum. but a proton has a **intrinsic angular momentum**, called **spin**, even though we should not picture it literally rotating like a little ball.

Wecan say that the spin of a proton is:

$$
S_z=\pm\frac{\hbar}{2}
$$

![Spin](/images/d24993725a7a7fca.jpg)

children.label: MRI Process
children.definition:
1. Hydrogen atoms are randomly oriented
2. Protons align with $B_0$ (Strong Magnetic Field)
3. A radiofrequency pulse (RF pulse) flips the magnetic moments of the protons to the transverse plane
4. After some $t$, the relax and return to equilibrium (same direction as $B_0$)

![MRI process](/images/d4ab6f2d44fafe1b.png)

children.label: What happens between transverse flip and relaxation?
children.definition: During this process the protons realign with $B_0$ and lose energy by **emitting their own RF signals**, which can be received using coils placed around he object being imaged.

children.label: Excitation during MRI process
children.definition:
During excitation, protons "jump" to a high energy level, and the net magnetic moment vector spirals down to the transverse plane. 

(Excitation happens when RF pulse arrives)

children.label: Relaxation in MRI Process
children.definition:
After excitation, the protons emit RF pulse of their own in the form of magnetic waves.

We have 2 types of relaxations:

- Longitudinal
- Transverse

children.label: T1 Relaxation
children.definition:
Is the relaxation parallel to $B_0$:

Is the process by which the net magnetisation returns to initial maximum value.

T1 relaxation is modeled as exponential growth curve with time constant T1. $M$ reaches $63\%$ of its maximum value ($M_0$) at $t=T1$ and is very close to maximal at $t=5\times T1$

![T1 Relaxation](/images/f65411e128b97fc1.png)

children.label: T1 Weighted MRI
children.definition:
Emphasises in **how quickly a tissue recovers its longitudinal magnetisation** after excitation. Tissues with short $T1$ recover fast and appear bright.

Lower T1 implies bright image
Higher T1 implies dark image

children.label: T2 Relaxation
children.definition:
Refers to the process that the transverse components of magnetisation decay or dephase

T2 is the time for $63\%$ of protons to lose precessional phase coeherence

![T2 elaxation](/images/6b893393daa4c0f1.png)

children.label: T2 Weighted MRI
children.definition:
Emphises on how quickly the transverse magnetisation decays:

- lower T2 implies dark images
- higher T2 implies bright images

children.label: MR Pulses
children.definition:
A single RF pulse generates a free induction decay, but 2 successive RF pulses produce a spin echo:

![Spin Echo Signal](/images/7de2349deda2e37a.png)

Spin Echo regenerates spin phase information apparently lost during the decay of the FID (free induction decay)

$90^\circ$ pulse tips the spins into the transverse plane; spins lose phase coherence; $180^\circ$ pulse refocuses he spins.

*Clinical MRI prefers spin echo sequences over raw Free Induction Decay (FID) signals primarily because FID suffers from rapid, uncontrollable signal loss and lacks the necessary image quality for diagnostic interpretation*.

children.label: Overall Signal Intensity
children.definition:
$$
S=K\cdot [H]\cdot (1-e^{-TR/T1})\cdot e^{-TE/T2}
$$

$K$ is a proportionality constant accounting for scanner and measurement factors, such as receiver-coil sensitivity and system gain.

children.label: TR (Repetition time)
children.definition:
Time between 90 degree RF pulse

![TR and TE](/images/690e43353ebbfda0.png)

children.label: TE (Echo Time)
children.definition:
The time between the initial 90 degree RF pulse and the echo

![TR and TE](/images/690e43353ebbfda0.png)

children.label: Types of MRI imaging according to TR and TE combinations
children.definition:
There are 4 types of MRI imaging outputs according to TR and TE combinations.

- T1 weighted
- T2 weighted
- PD weighted
- Poor contrast

![types of MRI table](/images/4588506521b8ce5d.png)

The T1-weighted sequence uses a short TR and
short TE (TR < 1000msec, TE < 30msec).

The T2-weighted sequence uses a long TR and
long TE (TR > 2000msec, TE > 80msec)

children.label: MRI Components
children.definition:
![MRI compoments](/images/64bf783468c6dc91.png)

4 main components:

- Magnetic field: usually given by a superconducting magnet (sometimes resistive or permanent magnet)

- Gradient coils: allow spatial encoding of the MR signal. When current is passed hrough these coils secondary magnetic field is created, mildly distort the main magnetic field in a predictable pattern, causing the resonance frequency of the protons to vary in as a function of position

- RF coil: function as the antennae for both transmitting signals
to and receiving signals from the tissue. They are located relatively close the patient’s
body. There are three basic types of RF coils, i.e., body, head and surface coils. The RF
pulses applied to a patient’s body are mostly absorbed by the tissue, while a small
amount of energy is emitted by the body to produce an image.

- Computer: include user interface, the Fourier transformer, the signal converter
and a preamplifier, etc.

children.label: Forming Images in MRI
children.definition: To separate signals from different part of the body we use spatial localisation. Magnetic gradients (slightly change main magnetic field) and Larmor frequency vary with positions to map parts of the body.

children.label: 3D localisation algorithm
children.definition:
1. Slice selected along z-axis
2. Intra-slice segment selected along x-axis by frequency encoding
3. Intra-slice segment selected along y-axis by phase encoding

children.label: Slice selection
children.definition:
Apply gradient to magnetic field on the $z$-axis

![Slice selection](/images/9968c869e83739ba.png)

children.label: Frequency Encoding Column selection
children.definition:
Recall the Larmor Frequency:

$$
\omega_0=\gamma B_0
$$

Alter the magnetic field with gradient $G_f$ (now $B$ is dependent on $x$ position):

$$
B(x) = B_0 + xG_f
$$

The resonant frequency $\omega(x)$ (larmor frequency) becomes a function of $x$:

$$
\omega(x)=\gamma \cdot B_0+\gamma\cdot x\cdot G_f = \omega_0+\omega_g(x)
$$ 

![pasted image](/images/efe6edd622a37067.png)

children.label: Phase encoding Row selection
children.definition:
![pasted image](/images/7d817dcb8df5918c.png)

Lets say we have 2 signals $A$ and $B$. Phase encoding lets us separate them:

- first measurement: both rows add so $s_0 = A+B$
- second measurement: row $B$ receives a $180^\circ$ phase shift, reversing its sign, so $S_1=A-B$.

We can isolate each row:

$$
\frac{S_0+S_1}{2}=A \text{ }(\text{Adding cancels row }B)
$$

$$
\frac{S_0-S_1}{2}=B \text{ }(\text{Adding cancels row }A)
$$

Thus, the rows are separated mathematically from combined measurements. For many rows, MRI uses many phase-encoding steps and an inverse **Fourier transform** to perform this separation.

children.label: K-space: raw data space of MRI signals
children.definition:
K-space is a matrix of numbers, representing the spatial frequency information in two or three dimensions of an object.

K-space = spatial Fourier transform 

![pasted image](/images/b53e75343dec26e2.png)

children.label: Restoring Image from K-space
children.definition:
**K-space stores the MRI measurements as spatial frequencies**: how rapidly image intensity varies across space. Each measurement combines signals from the whole slice.

Gradients give spins a position-dependent phase:

$$
\phi(x,y)=2\pi(k_xx+k_yy).
$$

The receiver measures their combined signal:

$$
S(k_x,k_y)=\iint m(x,y)\,e^{-i2\pi(k_xx+k_yy)}\,dx\,dy,
$$

where $m(x,y)$ is the image we want. **This equation is a 2D Fourier transform.**

To recover the image, apply the **inverse Fourier transform**:

$$
\boxed{m(x,y)=\mathcal F^{-1}_{2D}\{S(k_x,k_y)\}}.
$$

It reverses the phase encoding and combines measurements so that signals reinforce at their correct positions—extending your $A+B,\ A-B$ example to thousands of pixels.

In a standard acquisition, phase encoding chooses a **k-space row**, and frequency encoding samples along it. K-space’s **centre captures broad intensity variations**, while its **outer regions capture fine details and edges**.

[Source: MRI spatial encoding](https://larsonlab.github.io/MRI-education-resources/Spatial%20Encoding.html)

children.label: 3 Main Advantages and Disadvantages of MRI
children.definition:
**Advantages**:

1. **No exposure to radiation**, therefore can be safely used to people vulnerable to radiation effects, such as a pregnant women and babies.

2. Useful for scanning soft tissues structures and organs.

3. Can provide information about the blood circulation through the body and blood vessels.

**Disadvantages**:

1. Performed in an enclosed space with loud noise, so people who are claustrophobic are facing problems with MRI.

2. MRI scans are very expensive: a single scanner can cost million dollars.

3. People who have internal metal objects, such as surgical clips, plates or screws may not be eligible for an MRI xam due to its strong magnet.

children.label: Diffusion MRI
children.definition:
Diffusion weighted MRI generates contrast in MR images uses the diffusion of water molecules.

Molecular diffusion in tissues is not free and restricted by surrounding obstacles, e.b. fibers, membranes and macromolecules. Therefore, water molecule diffusion patterns can reveal microscopic details of tissue architecture

**Diffusion MRI (dMRI) is preferred not just for its absolute anatomical accuracy, but because it provides unique microscopic, functional, and structural connectivity information that conventional MRI cannot see**

![pasted image](/images/6d42c95ebaeca60e.png)

children.label: Brownian Motion
children.definition: **Brownian motion** is the random motion of particles suspended in a medium (a liquid or a gas).[2] The traditional mathematical formulation of Brownian motion is that of the Wiener process, which is often itself called "Brownian motion", even in mathematical sources.

children.label: Isoptropic Diffusion
children.definition:
Molecules has no restriction in movement

![pasted image](/images/e22b3cc1ae337bef.png)

children.label: Ansiotropic diffusion
children.definition:
Molecule is restricted to 1 primary direction:

![pasted image](/images/eab52e06a9b1c55d.png)

children.label: Spin echo equation for diffusion MRI
children.definition:
**Spin echo is a standard MRI method.** Your new equation adds the effect of **diffusion weighting** to the spin-echo equation you learned earlier.

Previously:

$$
S_0=K\cdot PD(1-e^{-TR/T_1})e^{-TE/T_2}
$$

With diffusion weighting:

$$
\boxed{S=S_0e^{-bD}}
$$

- **$b$:** Strength of the diffusion weighting, controlled by the diffusion gradients.
- **$D$:** Diffusion coefficient, describing how freely water molecules move.

Greater diffusion causes more signal loss. When $b=0$, the diffusion factor equals 1, giving the original spin-echo signal.

TR, TE and b are sequence dependent imaging parameters that could be controlled. Varying these parameters can change the contributions of T1, T2 and D terms.

children.label: Unerstanding b in dMRI equation
children.definition:
## Understanding b in the dMRI equation

![pasted image](/images/657363eb24ba05ae.png)

**The b-value controls how sensitive the signal is to water diffusion**, through the strength, duration and timing of the diffusion gradients.

The lower/higher-frequency arrows describe how gradients make spins at different positions precess at different rates:

- **Dephasing:** Spins accumulate different phases.
- **Rephasing:** The sequence cancels these phase differences for stationary spins.
- **With diffusion:** Water molecules change position, so cancellation is incomplete, reducing the measured signal.

$$
S=S_0e^{-bD}
$$

**Higher b means greater signal loss for the same diffusion coefficient $D$.** Restricted diffusion therefore retains more signal than freely diffusing water.

For two rectangular diffusion-gradient pulses:

$$
b=\gamma^2G^2\delta^2\left(\Delta-\frac{\delta}{3}\right),
$$

where $G$ is gradient strength, $\delta$ is pulse duration, and $\Delta$ is the time between pulse starts. Units are usually $\mathrm{s/mm^2}$.

[Source: ISMRM diffusion MRI acquisition basics](https://www.ismrm.org/dmff-uploads/2s.pdf)

children.label: How to measure diffusion
children.definition:
It is impossible to extract the information about diffusion orientation from a single intensity value, but we can retrieve it by analysing 2 images with different $b$ while other parameters remain the same.

$$
\begin{align}
S_1 &= PD(1-e^{-TR/T1})e^{-TE/T2}e^{-b_1D}\\
S_1 &= S_0e^{-b_1D} \\
S_2 &= S_0e^{-b_2D} \\
\frac{S_2}{S_1} &=e^{-(b_2-b_1)D} \\
\therefore \text{ } D &= -\ln\left( \frac{S_2}{S_1} \right) / (b_2-b_1)
\end{align}
$$

children.label: Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC)
children.definition:
By solving $D$ at each pixel, we can calculate a map of the diffusion coefficient, called **apparent diffusion coefficient**.

In ADC maps, the intensity of each pixel is proportional to the extent of diffusion: water molecules in birght regions diffuse faster than those in dark regions.

| Diffusion | DWI | ADC map |
|---|---|---|
| Low / restricted | Bright | Dark |
| High / unrestricted | Dark | Bright |

ADC maps are calculated by comparing signals acquired with different b-values, typically $b=0$ and a higher $b$:

$$
ADC=-\frac{1}{b}\ln\left(\frac{S_b}{S_0}\right)
$$

This is calculated **for each voxel**. Greater signal loss with diffusion weighting gives a higher ADC.

children.label: Why do ADC maps of different gradient orentations could be remarkably different?
children.definition:
Due to **ansiotropic diffusion**.

Water may move easily along one direction but be restricted along another. Therefore, changing the gradient direction can change the measured ADC in the same tissue.

If you point the gradient **across a fibre**, where water motion is more restricted, the signal usually **drops less** and the measured ADC is **lower** than when you point it along the fibre.

Only if there were **no motion at all** along that direction would there be no signal loss due to diffusion.

children.label: What does the argest ADC suggest?
children.definition:
Water generally diffuses more easily along *axonal fibres* than across them. The direction with the greatest ADC estimes the **dominant fibre orientation** 

*axonal fibres*
![pasted image](/images/94a8ee5c863b930e.png)

children.label: Is measuring X, Y, Z sufficient for full directional pattern of diffusion reconstruction? If not, what calculation is necessary for fiber orientation?
children.definition:
**NO**,  Fibres can point at any angle. Three axis measurements do not provide enough information to reconstruct the full directional pattern of diffusion.

**Tensor Calculation** is required to determine fiber orientation precisely.

children.label: Diffusion Tensor Imaging DTI
children.definition:
Advanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique that maps the 3D diffusion of water molecules to visualize the microstructural organization of white matter in the brain

![pasted image](/images/7f5d1d02e2bfdd59.png)

![pasted image](/images/018360260505edeb.png)

children.label: What does DTI measure and how?
children.definition:
Measurements of **how much water diffuses along different directions** in each voxel.

For each gradient direction, the scanner measures **signal loss** relative to a baseline and uses it to estimate a **directional ADC**. DTI combines these measurements to fit a 3D ellipsoid. Its longest axis points in the direction of greatest estimated diffusion.

The length and orientations of the longest,
middle and shortest axis of the ellipsoid can
be determined b six parameters organised in
to a 3x3 symmetric matrix called diffusion
tensor.

$$
\mathbf{D} =
\begin{bmatrix}
D_{xx} & D_{xy} & D_{xz} \\
D_{xy} & D_{yy} & D_{yz} \\
D_{xz} & D_{yz} & D_{zz}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

children.label: Eigen decompsition in DTI
children.definition:
**Eigendecomposition** tells you which way the diffusion ellipsoid points and how stretched it is along each of its three axes.

$$
\mathbf D\mathbf v_i=\lambda_i\mathbf v_i
$$

This means that applying the tensor $\mathbf D$ to an eigenvector $\mathbf v_i$ scales it by $\lambda_i$ while preserving its direction.

- **Eigenvector $\mathbf v_i$:** The direction of an ellipsoid axis.
- **Eigenvalue $\lambda_i$:** How much water diffuses along that axis.

The **largest eigenvalue** gives the greatest diffusivity. Its eigenvector points along the ellipsoid’s longest axis and estimates the dominant fibre orientation.

children.label: Indeces of diffusion
children.definition: Gives us information about the total diffusivity of the molecule.

children.label: Fractional anisotropy (FA)
children.definition:
**Fractional anisotropy (FA)** measures **how directional** diffusion is. FA is 0 when diffusion is equal in all directions and 1 when it occurs along only one axis.

$$
\mathrm{FA} = \sqrt{\frac{(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)^2+(\lambda_2-\lambda_3)^2+(\lambda_1-\lambda_3)^2}{2(\lambda_1^2+\lambda_2^2+\lambda_3^2)}}
$$

![pasted image](/images/b5f6d05a09f48bc1.png)

FA does not discriminate between ellipsoid
orientation. For example, the two ellipsoids below
have the same FA with different directions:

![pasted image](/images/b5ab6f01f3fe676c.png)

children.label: Mean diffusivity (MD)
children.definition:
**Mean diffusivity (MD)** measures **how much** water diffuses on average. It is the mean of the three principal diffusivities:

$$
\mathrm{MD} = \frac{\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3}{3}
$$

children.label: Deterministic Tratography
children.definition:
For estimation of white matter pathways and exploring which brain regons may connect, we can use **deterministic tractography**:

Follows one estimated fibre direction at each step. In DTI, that direction comes from the tensor’s principal eigenvector. It’s used to trace and visualise pathways.

1. Assume largest eigevector reflects dominant fibre orientation.
2. If $\mathrm{FA} < 0.15$:
   - stop tracking, else continue
3. If $\theta > 50^\circ$
   - stop tracking, else continue

The process does not allow branching fibers

children.label: Limits of Deterministic Tractography
children.definition:
1. Fiber path across voxel is inferred based on a single diffusion orientation of each voxel.
2. utilizing only one diffusion orientation per voxel may
not adequately characterize voxels
3. deterministic FT can follow false tracts or may stop in
regions with isotropic tensors

children.label: Probabilistic Fibre Tracking
children.definition:
For estimation of white matter pathways and exploring which brain regons may connect, we can use **Probabilistic Fibre Tracking**:

- dealing with the uncertainty along the track path
- propagate a large number of pathways from the seed point.

  - pathwys sample from he dstribution of directon
  - output: proportion of pathways from seed point reach a given voxel
  - high probability does not guarantee that the tract exists.

children.label: What is geometric distortion and how do you approach this
children.definition:
**Geometric distortion** means parts of an MRI image appear shifted, stretched or compressed because the scanner assigns the signal to the wrong location.

- **Gradient nonlinearity.** The scanner assumes the gradient field changes linearly with position. When it deviates from that straight-line relationship, the scanner miscalculates positions. A scanner calibration map can correct this warp.
- **Main field inhomogeneity ($B_0$).** The scanner assumes the main magnetic field is uniform. Local variations shift the precession frequency, which can be mistaken for a change in position. In diffusion MRI acquired with EPI, this distortion occurs mainly along the phase-encoding direction. A field map or images acquired with opposite phase-encoding directions can help undo it.

**Correct geometric distortion by estimating the warp and moving voxels back to their expected positions.** (Correction of geometric distortion often requires phantom scans (not
very commonly performed))

2. **Absorption**: The photon interacts and transfers all its energy to the tissues atoms (*Photoelectrical effect*).

A relatively low energy x-ray photon uses all its energy to eject an inner shell electron, leavin an orbital vacancy.

An electron from the shell above drops down to fill the vacancy and, in doing so, gives up energy in the form of a charateristic ray.

The **photoelectric effect** is more likely to occur in absorbers of high atomic number (like bones), and contributes significantly to patient dose, as all the photon energy is absorbed by the patient.

children.label: CT numbers
children.definition:
A **CT number ($h$)** measures how strongly a voxel attenuates X-rays relative to water. It is expressed in **Hounsfield units (HU)**.

$$
h = 1000\,\frac{\mu_{\text{voxel}}-\mu_{\text{water}}}{\mu_{\text{water}}}
$$

Here, $\mu$ is the linear attenuation coefficient.

- **Air:** approximately $-1000$ HU
- **Water:** $0$ HU
- **Dense bone:** often around $+1000$ HU or higher

A higher CT number means stronger X-ray attenuation.

children.label: X-ray photon equations in CT
children.definition:
$N_i$ is the number of incident X-ray photons, $N_o$ is the number transmitted, and $\mu$ is the linear attenuation coefficient.

1. **One layer.** For a uniform layer of thickness $\Delta x$, the fraction of photons that pass through is $e^{-\mu\Delta x}$:

   $$
   N_o=N_i e^{-\mu\Delta x}.
   $$

![pasted image](/images/dfea91b9e3b00557.png)

2. **Several layers.** Each layer attenuates the photons that survived the previous one. The fractions multiply, so the exponents add. For three layers of equal thickness:

   $$
   N_o=N_i e^{-(\mu_1+\mu_2+\mu_3)\Delta x}.
   $$

![pasted image](/images/14f851f0b0bcf73b.png)


3. **Any number of layers.** Replace the three terms with a sum, then take the natural log of the incident-to-transmitted ratio:

   $$
   N_o=N_i e^{-\sum_k\mu_k\Delta x}
   \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
   \ln\frac{N_i}{N_o}=\sum_k\mu_k\Delta x.
   $$

4. **Continuously varying tissue.** As the layers become infinitesimally thin, the sum becomes an integral along the ray:

   $$
   \ln\frac{N_i}{N_o}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mu(x)\,\mathrm dx.
   $$

**In CT, each ray gives one total attenuation value.** The scanner combines measurements from many rays and angles to reconstruct the local $\mu$ values in the image.

children.label: CT projections
children.definition:
The total X-ray attenuation along one ray through a CT slice. This is the $\ln(N_i/N_o)$.

The first equation **adds up attenuation along the ray**:

$$
p_\theta(t)=\int_{(\theta,t)\,\text{line}}\mu(x,y)\,ds.
$$

Here, $\mu(x,y)$ is the local attenuation, $\theta$ sets the ray’s orientation, $t$ is its signed offset from the origin, and $ds$ is a small step along the ray.

The second equation writes the same calculation as an integral over the whole slice. The **Dirac delta** $\delta(x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta-t)$ selects only points on the ray:

$$
x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta=t.
$$

For example, if $\theta=0$, the ray is the vertical line $x=t$, so $p_0(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mu(t,y)\,dy$.

Varying $t$ at a fixed $\theta$ gives one **parallel projection**. Collecting projections at many angles gives the **Radon transform** data used to reconstruct the CT slice.

![pasted image](/images/bfaf6f8a50596b66.png)

children.label: Fourier Slice Theorem in CT
children.definition:
**From a projection to a Fourier slice.** At a fixed angle $\theta$, the CT projection $p_\theta(t)$ records the total attenuation along each of a set of parallel rays. Taking the **1D Fourier transform** of that projection gives one line through the centre of the image’s **2D Fourier spectrum**:

   $$
   \mathcal F_{1D}\{p_\theta\}(\omega)
   =\widehat{\mu}(\omega\cos\theta,\omega\sin\theta).
   $$

   Here, $\theta$ is the angle of the detector axis, perpendicular to the X-ray rays.

![pasted image](/images/3d1eb45f7c0d868a.png)

children.label: How CT reconstructs an image
children.definition:
**From Fourier slices back to the CT image.** Repeat this at many angles. Each angle gives a different line in the 2D Fourier spectrum. Interpolate those samples onto a rectangular grid, then apply a **2D inverse FFT** to recover the attenuation image $\mu(x,y)$

![pasted image](/images/40552a37b01142c4.png)

children.label: Fourier-domain Reconstruction
children.definition: ![pasted image](/images/cb1caa93a86c1d46.png)

children.label: Projection and Backprojection in CT scans
children.definition:
The backprojection process can be expressed mathematically. The reconstructed back-projection image $b_\theta(x,y)$ at a particular viw $\theta$ is:

$$
b_\theta(x,y)=\int p_\theta(t)\delta(x\cos \theta + y \sin \theta -t)\mathrm{d} t
$$

Adding up the images at all angles $(0,\pi)$:

$$
\begin{align}
f_b(x,y)&=\int_0^\pi b_\theta(x,y)\mathrm{d}\theta\\
&= \int_0^\pi \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p_\theta(t)\delta(x\cos \theta + y \sin \theta -t)\mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d}\theta
\end{align}
$$

children.label: Gradient Based Edge Detection
children.definition:
The gradient of an image is given by:

$$
\nabla f = \left[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x},\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right]
$$

The gradient points in the direction of the most rapid change intensity. And its direction is given by:

$$
\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(  \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}/\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right)
$$

The edge strength is given by the gradient magnitude:

$$
\|\nabla f\|
$$

children.label: Prewitt Operator edge based segmentation
children.definition:
Prewitt operator: is sensitive to noise when compared to sobel operator:

- Calculate the Horizontal and Vertical edges of irignal image $A$:

$$
\mathbf{G_x}=\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&-1\\1&0&-1\\1&0&-1
\end{bmatrix} * A \text{ and } \mathbf{G_y} = \begin{bmatrix} 1&1&1\\0&0&0\\-1&-1&-1 \end{bmatrix} * A
$$

Combine the 2 edges into final gradient magnitude:

$$
\mathbf{G}=\sqrt{\mathbf{G_x}^2+\mathbf{G_y}^2}
$$

![pasted image](/images/186980f8b58884f9.png)

children.label: Sobel operator edge based segmentation algorithm
children.definition:
**Most commonly used** to emphasize edges. Really similar to prewitt operator:

Calculate the horizontal and vertical edges of image $A$:

$$
\mathbf{G_x}=\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&-1\\1&0&-1\\1&0&-1
\end{bmatrix} * A \text{ and } \mathbf{G_y} = \begin{bmatrix} 1&1&1\\0&0&0\\-1&-1&-1 \end{bmatrix} * A
$$

Combien the 2 edges into a final gradient magnitude

$$
\mathbf{G} = \sqrt{\mathbf{G_x}^2+\mathbf{G_y}^2}
$$

children.label: K-Means
children.definition:
**K-means** divides $n$ objects into $K$ groups based on their attributes. Each object is represented by a vector $x_i$, and each group has a centre called its **centroid** $\mu_j$.

1. **Choose $K$.** Decide how many groups you want.
2. **Initialise the centroids.** Pick $K$ starting centres, for example by choosing $K$ data points.
3. **Measure distances.** Calculate the distance from each object to every centroid.
4. **Group by nearest centroid.** Assign each object to the group whose centroid is closest.
5. **Check whether any object changed groups.** If none did, stop. Otherwise, recalculate each centroid as the **mean of the objects now in its group**, then return to step 3.

![pasted image](/images/556e7ca88ffc6101.png)

The objective is

$$
J=\sum_{j=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in S_j}\|x_i-\mu_j\|^2.
$$

For each object, this adds its **squared distance to its own group's centroid**. Assigning objects to their nearest centroid reduces this cost for the current centres. Recalculating the means reduces it for the current groups.

**Patch-based classification labels each pixel using a small window around it.** The neighbouring pixels give the classifier context, so two pixels with the same intensity can get different labels if their surroundings look different.

1. **Extract a patch.** Take a small window, such as $5\times5$ pixels, centred on the pixel you want to label. Slide the window one pixel at a time, so adjacent patches overlap.
2. **Extract features.** Describe what the patch contains, for example its average intensity, texture or edges.
3. **Classify the patch.** Use those features to predict a class, such as grey matter or white matter.
4. **Label the centre pixel.** Assign the prediction to the centre pixel. The other 24 pixels provide context.
5. **Build the segmentation.** Repeat across the image and put each predicted label in its original pixel location.

Its a supervised learning methods that assumes bayes theorem. It involves both, categorical and continuous valued attributes.

**Bayes Theorem**

$$
P(b|a) = \frac{P(a|b)P(b)}{P(a)}

**Its definition as a classifier**

X:(x_1,x_2,...,x_n)
$$

- Let there are

children.label: Why use Naive Bayes Classifier and how does it work?
children.definition:
**Naive Bayes classifies a patch by asking how likely its features are under each possible class.** For MRI segmentation, the feature vector $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ could contain the patch’s mean intensity and texture, and $C_i$ could be a tissue class such as grey matter.

The chain rule lets us break down the joint likelihood $P(X\mid C_i)$. With just two features:

$$
P(x_1,x_2\mid C_i)=P(x_1\mid x_2,C_i)\,P(x_2\mid C_i).
$$

The first term asks how likely $x_1$ is when we know **both** the class and the value of $x_2$. With many features, these combinations are hard to estimate from limited training data.

Naive Bayes assumes that **once the class is known, the features are independent**. Under this assumption, knowing the texture adds no information about the intensity within that tissue class. So we can learn one distribution per feature per class and multiply their likelihoods:

$$
P(X\mid C_i)=\prod_{k=1}^{n}P(x_k\mid C_i).
$$

**How it learns and predicts.** During training, labelled patches tell us which class each example belongs to. We use them to estimate the class prior $P(C_i)$ and each feature’s distribution within that class. For a new patch, we pick the class with the highest score:

$$
\widehat C=\arg\max_{C_i}\left[P(C_i)\prod_{k=1}^{n}P(x_k\mid C_i)\right].
$$

Bayes’ rule divides each score by the same $P(X)$, so we can skip that division when choosing the winning class.

**Why it works well as a baseline.** Learning each feature separately requires fewer parameters than modelling all their relationships. That makes training and prediction fast and can help when labelled examples are limited. The trade-off is that strongly correlated features can effectively count the same evidence twice, making the model overconfident.

children.label: Linear SVM
children.definition:
**A linear SVM draws a boundary between two classes and chooses the boundary with the widest gap between them.** In two dimensions the boundary is a line. With more features, it is called a hyperplane.

SVMs find a hyperplane to separate 2 category data, and it maximises the margin, which is the distance between the canonical hyperplane

### 1. How the boundary classifies a point

For an input feature vector $\mathbf{x}$, the classifier computes

$$
g(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{w}^{T}\mathbf{x}+w_0.
$$

The weights $\mathbf{w}$ determine the boundary’s orientation, and the bias $w_0$ shifts its position. The boundary itself is where $g(\mathbf{x})=0$. A positive score predicts class $+1$, and a negative score predicts class $-1$.

For example, if $\mathbf{x}$ contains a patch’s **mean intensity** and **texture**, each patch is a point on a 2D plot. Its predicted class depends on which side of the line it falls on.

### 2. What the training constraint means

$$
y_i\bigl(\mathbf{w}^{T}\mathbf{x}_i+w_0\bigr)>0
\qquad \text{for every training point } i.
$$

This checks that the score and the true label have the **same sign**. A $+1$ point needs a positive score. A $-1$ point needs a negative score. In either case their product is positive.

### 3. What makes it an SVM

Several lines might classify every training point correctly. The SVM chooses the one that **maximises the distance to the closest training points**. Those closest points are the **support vectors**.

We can scale $\mathbf{w}$ and $w_0$ without moving the boundary, so the SVM sets the two edges of the margin at $g(\mathbf{x})=+1$ and $g(\mathbf{x})=-1$. The total width between them is $2/\|\mathbf{w}\|$. Thus, a **hard-margin SVM** solves

$$
\min_{\mathbf{w},\,w_0}\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2
\qquad
\text{subject to }
y_i\bigl(\mathbf{w}^{T}\mathbf{x}_i+w_0\bigr)\ge 1
\quad \forall i.
$$

When the classes overlap, a **soft-margin SVM** allows some points inside the margin or on the wrong side of the boundary, with a penalty for those violations.

![pasted image](/images/7e8ca1eefa96e346.png)

children.label: Classification Margin of SVM
children.definition:
The criteria with margin:

$$
y_i(w^tx_i+w_0)\geq b
$$

All data points at a distance greater than $\frac{b}{\|w\|}$ from the separating hyperplane.

It is convenient to make $b=1$.

This defines the canonical hyperplanes:

$$
\begin{align}
&H1:w^tx_i+w_0=+1\\
&H2:w^tx_i+w_0=-1\\
\end{align}
$$

and the constraints are:

$$
\begin{align}
&w^tx_i+w_0\geq+1 \text{ for }y_i=+1\\
&w^tx_i+w_0\leq+1 \text{ for }y_i=-1\\
\end{align}
$$

children.label: Prime Optimisation of Hard-margin SVM
children.definition:
## Primal optimisation of a hard-margin SVM

The **primal optimisation problem** minimises over both the weight vector $\mathbf{w}$ and the intercept $w_0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\mathbf{w},w_0}\quad &\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2\\
\text{subject to}\quad &y_i(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_i+w_0)\geq 1
\qquad \text{for every } i.
\end{aligned}
$$

To match the convention $g_i\leq 0$, write each constraint as

$$
g_i(\mathbf{w},w_0)=1-y_i(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_i+w_0)\leq 0.
$$

With one multiplier $\alpha_i\geq 0$ per training example, the **primal Lagrangian** is

$$
\mathcal{L}_p(\mathbf{w},w_0,{\alpha})
=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2
+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i
\left[1-y_i(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_i+w_0)\right].
$$

The equivalent Lagrangian form of the primal problem is

$$
\min_{\mathbf{w},w_0}\ \sup_\alpha\geq 0}
\mathcal{L}_p(\mathbf{w},w_0,\alpha).
$$

At a feasible $(\mathbf{w},w_0)$, the inner supremum is attained at
\alpha=\mathbf{0}$ and equals $\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$.
If any constraint is violated, its multiplier can grow without bound,
making the inner supremum $+\infty$. This is how the inner optimisation
enforces the hard-margin constraints.

children.label: Optimisation Problem Solution of a Linear SVM
children.definition:
**What a linear SVM learns during training** and how it uses that result to classify a new point. Here, $b$ is the bias, previously called $w_0$.

1. **The support vectors determine the boundary.** Training gives each point $\mathbf{x}_i$ a nonnegative weight $\alpha_i$. The SVM builds the boundary’s normal vector as

   $$
   \mathbf{w}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i y_i\mathbf{x}_i.
   $$

   Points with $\alpha_i=0$ contribute nothing to the sum. Points with $\alpha_i>0$ are the **support vectors**. In a hard-margin SVM, they lie on the edges of the margin.

2. **A support vector fixes the bias.** A support vector $\mathbf{x}_k$ on the margin has a score of $+1$ or $-1$, matching its label $y_k$. So

   $$
   \mathbf{w}^{T}\mathbf{x}_k+b=y_k
   \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
   b=y_k-\mathbf{w}^{T}\mathbf{x}_k.
   $$

   For this step, choose a point with **$\alpha_k>0$**. The slide’s $\alpha_i\geq 0$ is the general constraint on the weights.

3. **A new point is classified using dot products.** Substitute the sum for $\mathbf{w}$ into the decision function:

   $$
   f(\mathbf{x})
   =\sum_{i:\,\alpha_i>0}\alpha_i y_i
   \bigl(\mathbf{x}_i^{T}\mathbf{x}\bigr)+b.
   $$

   Each support vector contributes a dot product with the new point, weighted by $\alpha_i$ and signed by its class $y_i$. The **sign of the final score** determines the predicted class.

children.label: What is PET (Positron Emission Tomography)?
children.definition:
PET is a noninvasive diagnostic imaging technique for measuring the metabolic activity of cells in the human body. (**Funcitonal Imaging**)

PET measures the 2 annihilation photons that are produced back-to-back after positron emission from a radionuclide tagged tracer molecule.

![pasted image](/images/fc6dd0200166521a.png)

children.label: Characteristics of PET (3)
children.definition:
- Only extremely small amounts of imaging substrate need to be injected because of the high sensitivity of PET.
- Many isotopes can be incorporated into biological substrates (glucose, $H_2O$, $NH_3$, $CO_2$, $O_2$, etc.) and pharmaceuticals, without altering their biological activity.
- Compared to CT images, PET images appear much blurrier and or noisier:

   - Spatial resolution of CT: $1\mathrm{mm}$
   - Spatial resolution of PET: $4-5\mathrm{mm}$

A(t)=A(0)e^{-t(\ln 2/\tau)} \text{ }\tau\text{ is half life of the nuclide}

children.label: Annihilation of positron and electron
children.definition:
**PET maps where a radioactive tracer accumulates** by detecting pairs of photons.

1. **Positron emission.** A radioactive nucleus in the tracer decays and emits a positron ($\beta^+$), the positively charged counterpart of an electron.
2. **Travel through tissue.** The positron travels a short distance, scattering and losing energy along the way.
3. **Annihilation.** The positron meets an electron. Their annihilation typically produces two photons, each with an energy of $511\,\mathrm{keV}$, travelling in nearly opposite directions.
4. **Coincidence detection.** When two detectors register the photons almost simultaneously, the scanner estimates that the annihilation occurred somewhere along the line connecting them. It combines many such detections to reconstruct the tracer distribution.

![pasted image](/images/af4378dd39255066.png)

children.label: How does PET work?
children.definition:
PET is a gamma ray imaging technique that uses radiotracers that emit positrons. The gamma rays used for imaging are produced when a positron meets an electron inseide the patients body, which annihilates both electron and positron and produces two gamma rays travelling in opposite directions.

The dominant annihilation photon interaction in human tissue is Compton scatter. The photon experiences a loss of energy and an associated change of direction, typically out of the detector, and so is unavailable for image formation.

children.label: Scattered Coincidence PET
children.definition:
A scattered coincidence in a Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scan occurs when at least one of the two 511-keV annihilation photons undergoes Compton scattering inside the patient's body before being detected. **This makes the scan understand the anhilitation photon in a wrong line**.

children.label: Detector Properties of PET
children.definition:
- Spatial Resolution
- Energy Resolution
- Time Resolution

children.label: Spatial resolution PET
children.definition:
PET directly controls spatial resolution in reconstructed image.

- Detector size is between $1$ to $5$ $\mathrm{mm}$.
- Light output: the number of scintillation photons produced by each incident photon.

*Scintillation*: brief light emission.

children.label: Energy resolution PET
children.definition:
**Energy resolution describes how precisely the detector measures a photon’s energy.**

- **Why it matters.** An unscattered PET photon has an energy of $511\,\mathrm{keV}$. Compton scattering in tissue changes its direction and lowers its energy. Accepting it can place the detected event along the wrong line.
- **Better energy resolution** helps distinguish these lower-energy photons from $511\,\mathrm{keV}$ photons. The scanner rejects events outside its accepted energy range, reducing scattered coincidences.
- **Light output.** The detector crystal converts deposited energy into light. More detected light generally gives a more precise energy estimate.
- **Intrinsic crystal resolution.** Even equal-energy photons produce slightly different light signals. Greater consistency gives better energy resolution.

children.label: Time Resolution PET
children.definition: Affects acceptance of random coincidences. Therefore we admit intervals of photon detection between $1$ to $10$ $\mathrm{ns}$. Depends on the decay time of the scintillation in the crystal and the processing time of the PMT signals.

children.label: 2D vs 3D Acquisitions in PET
children.definition:
PET scanners may or may not utilise collimation.

1. If collimation is used, all data is acquaried in 2D slices. THe slices can be stacked and represented as 3D information.

   - **Lower sensitivity and easier to reconstruct**

2. Without collimation, coincidences from all axial angles in the field of volumen will be accepted, making a fully 3D aqcuisition.

   - **Higher sensitivity and harder to reconstruct**

![pasted image](/images/eb94d2388d064038.png)

children.label: Image Formation
children.definition:
1. **Identify lines of response (LORs).**  
   Each detected coincidence defines a line connecting two detectors. The annihilation is assumed to have occurred somewhere along that line.

2. **Form projections.**  
   Group the counts from parallel LORs at the same angle. Together, they form a projection showing how detected activity varies across that direction.

3. **Build the sinogram.**  
   Arrange projections from different angles into rows. Each row represents one angle. A single point of activity traces a sinusoidal curve across the sinogram.

4. **Correct for attenuation.**  
   Some photons are absorbed or scattered before reaching the detectors, reducing the recorded counts. Use a transmission scan or a CT-derived attenuation map to compensate and estimate tracer uptake more accurately.

5. **Reconstruct the tracer distribution.**  
   The slides present three alternative approaches:

| Method | How it forms the image |
|---|---|
| **Fourier reconstruction** | Fourier-transform each projection, place it into the 2D spectrum using the central slice theorem, then apply an inverse transform. |
| **Filtered back projection (FBP)** | Filter the projections to compensate for blurring, then spread each projection back along its LORs and combine them. |
| **Iterative reconstruction, such as OSEM** | Start with an estimated image, predict its projections, compare them with the measured data, and repeatedly update the image. It can incorporate noise and detector models. |

The final slide compares FBP and OSEM images. The OSEM example shows fewer visible streak artefacts.

children.label: Linear model and Dimensionality reduction in feature extraction and selection of MIA
children.definition:
**Dimensionality reduction represents each object using fewer features**, reducing computation and potentially removing redundant or irrelevant information.

If an object initially has $N$ features, we want a representation with $M<N$ features while preserving information useful for the task.

For a column vector $\mathbf{x}_i$, your scalar linear model is

$$
f(\mathbf{x}_i)=\mathbf{w}^{T}\mathbf{x}_i+w_0.
$$

Only $\mathbf{w}$ is transposed so that the multiplication produces a scalar.

### 1. Feature extraction

**Create new features from the original ones.** In linear feature extraction, each new feature is a weighted combination:

$$
y_j=\sum_{k=1}^{N}w_{kj}x_k+b_j.
$$

Collecting $M$ such combinations gives

$$
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{W}^{T}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b},
\qquad
\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M}.
$$

For example, two correlated intensity measurements might be combined into one feature:

$$
y_1=\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}.
$$

- **PCA** chooses combinations that preserve as much variation in the data as possible.
- **LDA** uses class labels to find combinations that separate classes.

The new features can capture patterns spread across several measurements, although their meaning may be harder to interpret.

### 2. Feature selection

**Keep a subset of the original features.** Their definitions and values stay the same.

For example, from a patch described by mean intensity, variance, texture and edge strength, we might keep only

$$
\mathbf{y}=
\begin{bmatrix}
\text{mean intensity}\\
\text{texture}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Features can be selected based on how informative they are about the class, how redundant they are with other features, or how well a classifier performs with them.

The selected features retain their original interpretation, but discarded features cannot contribute to the classifier.

Both approaches usually lose some information. Their success depends on preserving the information needed for the classification task.

children.label: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
children.definition:
**PCA is a feature extraction technique**

For $N$ data samples:

$$
\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2,\cdots,\mathbf{x}_N
$$

Find a projection with direction $\mathbf{u}$. After projection, we obtain a new set of features that are the linear combination of the original features:

$$
u(\mathbf{x}_i)=\mathbf{u}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}_i)
$$

*Find the direction* $\mathbf{u}$ so that after the projection, data variance could be maximally preserved.

---

**You are choosing a line onto which all the data points will be projected.** The vector $\mathbf{u}$ specifies that line’s direction.

For each point $\mathbf{x}_i$, the dot product

$$
z_i=\mathbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{x}_i
$$

gives its **coordinate along the line**. A point with several features is therefore represented by one number.

Imagine an elongated cloud of points:

- Projecting along its **long direction** keeps the projected points spread apart.
- Projecting across its **narrow direction** bunches them together, losing much of their variation.

PCA chooses the direction that gives the **largest variance of the projected coordinates**.

After centring the data, this is

$$
\begin{align}
\text{Maximise variance } var(u) &= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\mathbf{u}^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\mu)(\mathbf{u}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}_i-\mu))^{\top}\\
&=\mathbf{u}^\top\sum\mathbf{u} 
\end{align}
$$

The condition $\|\mathbf{u}\|=1$ fixes the vector’s length, so we compare directions fairly. Otherwise, simply making $\mathbf{u}$ longer would increase the projected variance.

The winning direction is the **first principal component**.

children.label: Optimisation Problem PCA
children.definition:
$$
\begin{align}
&\max \mathbf{u}^\top\sum\mathbf{u} \\
&\text{subject to }\|\mathbf{u}\|=1
\end{align}
$$

Using Lagrange multiplier:

$$
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u},\lambda) = \mathbf{u}^\top\sum\mathbf{u}+\lambda(1-\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u})
$$

### How does PCA know the line fits the data?

PCA takes the 1st random line that goes through the origin and projects the data point to the line. And then it can either measure the distances from the data to the line and try to minimise those distances or it can try to find the line that maximises the distances from the projected points to the origin.

$$

### Now, how to do PC2?

children.label: Linear Separability Problem
children.definition: The linear separability problem is the task of determining whether two classes of data points can be completely separated by a straight line (in 2D) or a flat hyperplane (in higher-dimensional spaces)

children.label: Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP)
children.definition:
![pasted image](/images/506bb3bd7f49f9a6.png)

## MLP

Solves the linear separability problem.

It has an objective $J(\mathbf{W})$ and an architecture of the form: input ($\mathbf{x}$) $\rightarrow$ hidden layers ($\mathbf{h}=f(\mathbf{W}_1\mathbf{x})$) $\rightarrow$ Output ($\mathbf{y}=f(\mathbf{W}_2\mathbf{h})$).

The ativation function will be gven by all the related functions:

$$
f=(f_n\circ f_{n-1}\cdots\circ f_1)(\mathbf{x})
$$

An MLP is a feedforward network of **fully connected layers**. Each layer applies a weighted sum, adds a bias and then applies activation. With one hidden layer:

$$
\begin{align}
\mathbf{h}=\phi_1(\mathbf{W_1}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}_1), \ \mathbf{\hat{y}} = \phi_2(\mathbf{W_2}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}_2)
\end{align}
$$

The nonlinear hidden activation $\phi_1$, such as ReLU, lets MLP learn nonlinear decision boundaries. The output activation depends on the task: sigmoid for binary classification, softmax for mutually exclusive classes or a linear outpur for regression.

During training, the loss compares the prediction $\mathbf{\hat{y}}$ with the true target $\mathbf{y}$. The objectiev $J$ typically averages that loss over the training examples. **Backpropagation** computes how the objective changes with each weight and bias, and an optimiser uses thos gradients to update parameters.

children.label: Objective Functions
children.definition:
**Least square loss for regression**:

$$
J(\mathbf{w})=\sum_i(y_i-p_i)^2+0.5\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2
$$

$0.5\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$ is a regularisation term. Magnitude of $\mathbf{w}$ should not be too large.

**Cross-entropy loss for multi-class classification**:

$$
J(\mathbf{w})=-\sum_i\sum_c y_{i,c}\log p_{i,c}+0.5\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2, \ y_{i,c}=1 \text{ or }0, \ \sum_cy_{i,c}=1
$$

$$
p(c_k=1|\mathbf{x}_i)=\frac{e^{o_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^ce^{o_j}}
$$

children.label: Forward phase of MLP Training
children.definition:
## Forward phase of MLP training

The forward pass uses the current weights and biases to turn an input $\mathbf{x}$ into a prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, then measures how far that prediction is from the target $\mathbf{y}$.

1. **Feed in the input.** The input features are the starting values:

   $$
   \mathbf{h}^{(0)}=\mathbf{x}.
   $$

2. **Compute each hidden layer.** For layer $\ell$, take a weighted sum of the previous layer’s outputs, add a bias, and apply the activation:

   $$
   \mathbf{z}^{(\ell)}
   =\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{h}^{(\ell-1)}+\mathbf{b}^{(\ell)},
   \qquad
   \mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}=\phi_\ell(\mathbf{z}^{(\ell)}).
   $$

   Here, $\mathbf{z}^{(\ell)}$ is the vector **before activation**, and $\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}$ is the vector passed to the next layer. Repeat for every hidden layer.

3. **Calculate the prediction.** If $L$ is the output layer, then

   $$
   \hat{\mathbf{y}}
   =\phi_L\!\left(\mathbf{W}^{(L)}\mathbf{h}^{(L-1)}+\mathbf{b}^{(L)}\right).
   $$

   For example, a sigmoid gives a probability $\hat y$ for the positive class in binary classification.

4. **Calculate the loss for each example.** Compare the prediction with its true target. For binary classification, binary cross-entropy is

   $$
   \mathcal{L}(y,\hat y)
   =-\left[y\log(\hat y)+(1-y)\log(1-\hat y)\right].
   $$

5. **Average the losses to obtain $J$.** For a batch of $B$ examples,

   $$
   J(\theta)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\mathcal{L}(y_i,\hat y_i),
   $$

   where $\theta$ contains all weights and biases. The backward pass then computes the gradients of $J$ with respect to those parameters.

![pasted image](/images/108aac5526f5e314.png)

children.label: Example Forward Phase 1
children.definition:
## Forward phase — worked example

We’ll predict whether an image patch contains a lesion using two features, one hidden ReLU neuron, and one sigmoid output neuron. The input is $\mathbf{x}=(2,1)^\top$, and the true label is $y=1$.

1. **Feed in the input.** The starting values are $\mathbf{h}^{(0)}=\mathbf{x}=(2,1)^\top$.

2. **Compute the hidden neuron.** Its weights are $(0.50,-0.25)$ and its bias is $0.25$. Multiply each input by its weight, add the bias, then apply ReLU:

   $$
   z^{(1)}=0.50(2)-0.25(1)+0.25=1,
   \qquad
   h^{(1)}=\max(0,z^{(1)})=1.
   $$

3. **Calculate the prediction.** The output weight is $0.80$ and its bias is $-0.80$. Apply sigmoid to the output score:

   $$
   z^{(2)}=0.80(1)-0.80=0,
   \qquad
   \hat y=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z^{(2)}}}=0.50.
   $$

   The network predicts a $50\%$ probability of a lesion.

4. **Calculate the loss.** Since the true label is $y=1$, binary cross-entropy becomes

   $$
   \mathcal{L}=-[y\log(\hat y)+(1-y)\log(1-\hat y)]
   =-\log(0.50)\approx0.693.
   $$

5. **Calculate the batch objective.** The objective $J$ is the average loss. Here the batch has one example, so $J=\mathcal{L}\approx0.693$.

![pasted image](/images/503678812e6211cf.png)

### 1. Feed in the training example (slide 13)

The diagram has two separate inputs. The feature vector $\mathbf{x}$ goes through the network to produce a prediction. The target $\mathbf{y}$ goes straight to the loss.

For example, an image patch could have two measured features, $\mathbf{x} = (2, 1)^\top$. If it belongs to class 2 out of three classes, its one-hot target is $\mathbf{y} = (0, 1, 0)^\top$.

### 2. Compute the first hidden layer (slide 14)

Each row of $\mathbf{W}^1$ contains the weights for one hidden neuron. That neuron multiplies the input features by its weights and adds the results. ReLU then replaces a negative result with zero and keeps a positive result as it is.

For example, with two hidden neurons:

$$
\mathbf{h}^1 = \operatorname{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}^1 \mathbf{x})
= \operatorname{ReLU}\left(
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
\right)
= \operatorname{ReLU}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$

The first neuron passes a value of $1$ to the next layer. The second passes $0$.

> **Note:** This follows the diagram, which leaves the biases out of the equations.

### 3. Compute the second hidden layer (slide 15)

This layer repeats the same operation, using $\mathbf{h}^1$ as its input. It learns combinations of what the first layer has already detected:

$$
\mathbf{h}^2 = \operatorname{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}^2 \mathbf{h}^1)
= \operatorname{ReLU}\left(
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
\right)
= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

### 4. Produce one score per class (slide 16) - NO activation function

Each row of $\mathbf{W}^3$ combines the second hidden layer's outputs into a score for one class. These raw scores are called **logits**:

$$
\mathbf{o} = \mathbf{W}^3 \mathbf{h}^2
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

### 5. Convert socres to probabilities (slide 17)

Finally convert the scrores to probabilities and calculate the loss. Softmax exponentials each score and divides the sum of all exponentiated scores. This gives positive probabilities that add up to $1$:

$$
p(x_k|\mathbf{x})=\frac{e^{o_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^Ce^{o_j}}, \ \mathbf{p}\approx\begin{pmatrix}0.665\\0.245\\0.090\end{pmatrix}
$$

Class 1 has the highest probability, but the training labale says class 2. Cross entropy uses the probability assigned to that true class. Because the target is one hot, only the class 2 term contributes:

$$
J=-\sum_{j=1}^Cy_j\log p(c_j|\mathbf{x})=-\log (0.245)\approx 1.41
$$

children.label: Backward phase MLP training
children.definition:
## Backward phase of MLP training

The forward pass computes the prediction and loss. The **backward pass** uses the chain rule to find how each weight and bias affects that loss. **Gradient descent** then updates those parameters.

1. **Define the objective.** For a batch of $B$ examples, training aims to find the parameters $\theta$ (all weights and biases) that minimise the average loss:

   $$
   \theta^*=\arg\min_\theta J(\theta),
   \qquad
   J(\theta)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\mathcal{L}(y_i,\hat y_i).
   $$

2. **Start at the output layer.** For one example, define $\delta^{(L)}=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial z^{(L)}$. This measures how the loss changes when the output score **before activation** changes. For a sigmoid output with binary cross-entropy, it simplifies to

   $$
   \delta^{(L)}=\hat y-y.
   $$

3. **Work backwards through the hidden layers.** Use the next layer’s weights to pass its gradient back, then multiply by the derivative of the current layer’s activation:

   $$
   \delta^{(\ell)}
   =
   \left[(\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)})^\top\delta^{(\ell+1)}\right]
   \odot\phi_\ell'(\mathbf{z}^{(\ell)}).
   $$

   Here, $\odot$ means element-by-element multiplication. Repeat from the last hidden layer to the first.

4. **Find the weight and bias gradients.** For each layer and each example:

   $$
   \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}}
   =\delta^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{h}^{(\ell-1)})^\top,
   \qquad
   \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{b}^{(\ell)}}
   =\delta^{(\ell)}.
   $$

   Each weight gradient is the receiving neuron’s $\delta$ times the input to that weight. Average these gradients across the batch to get $\nabla_\theta J$.

5. **Update the parameters.** The gradient points toward increasing loss, so subtract it:

   $$
   \theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla_\theta J,
   $$

   where $\eta$ is the **learning rate**. The next forward pass uses the updated weights and biases.

![pasted image](/images/dd58b31eb329de1e.png)

children.label: Example Backward Phase 1
children.definition:
## Backward phase — worked example

Use the same network and training example. The forward pass gave $h^{(1)}=1$, $\hat y=0.50$, and $y=1$.

1. **Set the objective.** Adjust the weights and biases to reduce $J$. With this one-example batch, the gradients of $J$ are the gradients of the example’s loss $\mathcal{L}$.

2. **Start at the output.** With sigmoid and binary cross-entropy, the gradient with respect to the output score is

   $$
   \delta^{(2)}
   =\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z^{(2)}}
   =\hat y-y=0.50-1=-0.50.
   $$

3. **Pass the gradient back to the hidden neuron.** Multiply by the output weight and the derivative of ReLU. Since $z^{(1)}=1>0$, the ReLU derivative is $1$:

   $$
   \delta^{(1)}=0.80(-0.50)(1)=-0.40.
   $$

4. **Find the weight and bias gradients.** For each weight, multiply the receiving neuron’s $\delta$ by the input to that weight. A bias has an effective input of $1$, so its gradient is just $\delta$:

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   \text{Output weight:}\quad &(-0.50)(1)=-0.50,\\
   \text{Output bias:}\quad &-0.50,\\
   \text{Hidden weights:}\quad &(-0.40)(2,1)=(-0.80,-0.40),\\
   \text{Hidden bias:}\quad &-0.40.
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   With a larger batch, average each parameter’s gradient across the examples before updating.

5. **Update the parameters.** Use $\theta_{\mathrm{new}}=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}-\eta\nabla_\theta J$ with learning rate $\eta=0.10$:

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   \text{Output weight:}\quad &0.80-0.10(-0.50)=0.85,\\
   \text{Output bias:}\quad &-0.80-0.10(-0.50)=-0.75,\\
   \text{Hidden weights:}\quad &(0.50,-0.25)-0.10(-0.80,-0.40)=(0.58,-0.21),\\
   \text{Hidden bias:}\quad &0.25-0.10(-0.40)=0.29.
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   The next forward pass on the same example gives $\hat y\approx0.575$. The prediction moves closer to $y=1$, and the loss drops from $0.693$ to about $0.553$.

children.label: Example Backward Phase 2
children.definition:
The backward pass works from the loss back to the first layer. At each layer, it answers two questions: How does each weight affect the loss? And what gradient should we pass to the preceding layer?

Let's consider: 

- $\mathbf{x}=(2,1)^\top$
- $\mathbf{h}^1=(1,0)^\top$
- $\mathbf{h}^2=(2,1)^\top$
- $\mathbf{0}=(2,1,0)^\top$
- True class is class 2, so $\mathbf{y}=(0,1,0)^\top$

1. Start with the loss and apply the chain rule. A weight affects the loss indirectly. It changes a neuron's output, which changes the class probabilities, which changes the loss. The chain rule links those effects. For example, if $h$ affects $p$ and $p$ affects $J$, then:

$$
\frac{\partial J}{\partial h} = \frac{\partial J}{\partial p}\frac{\partial p}{\partial h}
$$

children.label: Learning Rate
children.definition:
The hyperoarameter $\alpha$ (lr) controls how much an MLP changes its weights and biases after backpropagation. Backpropagation computes the gradients, and gradients descent subtracts that gradient multiplied by $\alpha$:

- **Small lr**: requires many updates before reaching minimum
- **Large lr**: might overshoot the minimum point

$$
w_{\text{new}} = w_\text{old}-\alpha\frac{\partial J}{\partial w}
$$

In MLP example, one output weight started at $0$ and had a gradient of $-1.511$. With $\alpha=0.1$

$$
w_{\text{new}} = 0-0.1(-1.511)=0.1511
$$

The weight increases because its gradient is negative: increasing it locally reduces loss.

children.label: Cross Entropy
children.definition:
Cross entropy measures **how good the prediction is**. In MLP with one hot label, the loss is negative log of the probabilitu assigned to the true class:

$$
\mathcal{L}=-\log(p_{\text{true class}})
$$

children.label: Batch Gradient Descent
children.definition: Use all training samples to calculate the average gradient, then update the wieghts once. Each update uses the full dataset, so it can be expensive. (Accurate estimation but expensive)

children.label: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)
children.definition:
Consider one sample and use it to calculate the gradient for weight update in a single step. Noisy gradient estimation but converges fast for large datasets. 

It uses a randomly selected training sample.

children.label: SGD with momentum
Mini-Batch Gradient Descent
children.definition:
Consider a small and fixed number of training samples in each step for weight update.

- Balance between batch gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent.

children.label: Random Initialisation
children.definition:
`W = 0.01*np.random.randn(D,H)`

`W = 1*np.random.randn(D,H)`

2 main issues:

- Too small initial weights soon make the activations approach 0
- Too large initial weights soon make the activation exploded

children.label: Xavier initialisation
children.definition:
**Xavier initialisation draws a random weights with a scale matched to the layer's size**. It centers the weghts at 0 and sets their variance to:

$$
\text{Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{\text{in}}-n_\text{out}} \ \text{ where }n_{\text{in/out}} \text{ is the number of input and outputs of the NN}
$$

Compared with using the same arbitrary scal for every layer, Xavier helps heep **activations during the forward pass** and **gradients during the backward pass** from shrinking or growing too much at the start of training.

```
W = np.random.randn(fan_in, fan_out) / np.sqrt(fan_in)
```

Or the original:

```
W = np.random.randn(fan_in, fan_out) * np.sqrt(2 / (fan_in + fan_out))
```

children.label: Kaiming's initialisation (or He initialisation)
children.definition:
Its designed for layers that use ReLU. It draws weights with mean zero and variance $2/\text{fan_{in}}$:

```
W = np.random.randn(fan_in, fan_out) * np.sqrt(2 / fan_in)
```

children.label: Problems on MLP (3)
children.definition:
- Every output unit interacts with every input unit
- The number of weights grws largely with size of input image
- Pixels and distance are less correlated

children.label: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
children.definition:
A CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) learns to detect patterns in grid-like data such as images.

A convolutional layer slides a small filter (for example, \(3\times3\) weights) across the image. At each position, it computes a weighted sum of the nearby pixels. The results form a feature map showing where the filter responds strongly.

The same weights are reused at every position, so a filter can detect an edge wherever it appears in the image. Deeper layers combine simple patterns such as edges and textures into more complex features that the network can use for tasks like classification or segmentation.

**This reduces the amount of parameters needded to compute the NN analysis**

children.label: Sparse Connectivity
children.definition:
Sparse connectivity means each neuron of the NN in a convolutional layer, connects to a small neighbourhood in the previous layer. For example, a $3\times3$ filter on a grayscal image uses **9 neaby pixels** to compute each output value. That patch is the neuron's **receptive field**. The local connections let CNNs detect patterns such as edges and textures.

![pasted image](/images/200b360dc6a32354.png)

children.label: Receptive Field
children.definition:
A neuron is only connected to a local region of the input grid. The local region is known as the **receptive field** of the neuron. This field can be increased by stacking more layers:

![pasted image](/images/8c74e17a9bd28a92.png)

children.label: Weight Sharing in CNNs
children.definition:
CNNs apply the same filter at every spatial location. The input pixels change as the filter slides, but its weights stay the same.

A $3\times 3$ filter on a grayscal image learns $9$ weights in total, even if its applied at $1000$ locations. This saves parameters and lets the same filter detect a pattern such as an edge, wherever it appears.

children.label: Multiple filters in CNNs
children.definition: Multiple filters are useful, since even though each filter contains the same set of weights, they mifht capture different patterns. Each filter learns a differnt patter, such as vertical edge, horizontal edge or a texture. Each produces its own **feature map** showing where that pattern appears.

children.label: Translation invariance
children.definition: Because the same filter scans the while image, it can detect pattern wherever it appears. If the pattern moves, its response moves on the feature map too. That is **translation equivariance/invariance**. A later operation such as global pooling can summarise how strongly the pattern appears across the image, making the final prediction less sensitive to where it appears.

children.label: Strided Convolution vs Pooling (W_out formula)
children.definition:
Use strided convolution ($\text{stride} > 1$) could also reduce the size of feature maps:

$$
W_{\text{out}}=\left\lfloor\frac{W_{\text{in}}-W_\text{out} + 2 \times P}{S}\right\rfloor+1
$$

- The kernel weights are learnable in strided convolution; however pooling has no learnable parameters

1. $W_{\text{in}}$: is the input width before padding
2. $W_{\text{out}}$: is the output width (should be the kernel width $K$). Each valid kernel position produces one output value along that row.
3. $K$: kernel width (usually $3\times 3$)
4. $P$: padding on each side. Padding adds extra values to the edges of an input image or feature map. Usually $0$s.
5. $S$: is the stride, the number of pixels the kernel moves each step.

children.label: Fully Connected Layers (FC)
children.definition:
FC layers flatten feature maps for prediction, same as MLP in principle. (Used for output layers)
